
## Overview of linear regression

In linear regression, our fundamental objective is to explain the variability observed in the outcome variable ($Y$) using one or more explanatory variable ($X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k$). 

:::{.hide}
$$
\hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_{1i} + b_2 X_{2i} + \dots + b_k X_{ki}
$$
:::

It is crucial to know

- Does $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k$ really make explaination to $Y$
- How good is the model performance?


:::{.aside}
(Note on terminology: In some literature, notably British and econometrics, SSR is termed "Explained Sum of Squares" (ESS) and SSE is termed "Residual Sum of Squares" (RSS). Always check definitions in your specific context).
:::

## Quick summary


| Metric | Formula | Degrees of Freedom ($df$) | Conceptual Intuition |
| :- | :-- | :-- | :------ |
| **SST** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2$ | $n - 1$ | Total variation in the outcome $Y$ without using any predictors. |
| **SSR** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{Y}_i - \bar{Y})^2$ | $k$ | Variation accounted  by the regression model. |
| **SSE** | $\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2$ <br> $= \sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$ | $n - k - 1$ | Unexplained variation; sum of squared discrepancies between observed points and regression surface. |

:::{.aside}
- $n$ represents the sample size
- $k$ represents the number of predictors, excluding the intercept.
:::
---

## Goodness-of-Fit: $R^2$ 

$R^2$ (The coefficient of determination) quantifies the proportion of total variation in the response variable explained by the linear combination of predictors:

:::{.hide}

$$
R^2 = \frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}} = 1 - \frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}
$$
:::

**Interpretation Rules**

- **Range:** In standard OLS with an intercept, $0 \le R^2 \le 1$ (or $0\%$ to $100\%$).
- **Interpretation:** If $R^2 = 0.74$, exactly **74% of the variability in $Y$ is explained by the predictors** included in the model, while the remaining 26% is attributable to residual noise or omitted factors.
- **Limitation:** $R^2$ is non-decreasing with respect to the addition of predictors. Adding completely unrelated random noise variables will force $\text{SSE}$ to stay equal or decrease, artificially inflating $R^2$.

## Adjusted $R^2$ ($R^2_{\text{adj}}$)

The **Adjusted $R^2$** incorporates degrees of freedom to penalize excessive parameterization and prevent overfitting, :

:::{.hide}
$$
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \left[ \frac{\text{SSE} / (n - k - 1)}{\text{SST} / (n - 1)} \right] = 1 - \left( \frac{\text{MSE}}{\text{MST}} \right)
$$
:::

Alternatively expressed via $R^2$:
$$
R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (1 - R^2) \frac{n - 1}{n - k - 1}
$$

**Key Properties**

- Increases only if a newly added predictor reduces $\text{SSE}$ by a margin greater than what would be expected by pure chance.
- Can occasionally yield a negative value when model fit is negligible; in such cases, it is effectively interpreted as zero.


## $F$-Test for Model Significance

**$F$-Test** evaluates whether the collection of predictors collectively explains a statistically significant amount of variation.

**Hypotheses**

- **Null Hypothesis ($H_0$):** All slope coefficients are simultaneously zero.
  
:::{.hide}

$$
H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_k = 0
$$

:::

- **Alternative Hypothesis ($H_1$):** At least one slope coefficient is non-zero.
  
:::{.hide}

$$
H_1: \text{There is at least one} \beta_j \neq 0
$$

:::

**Difference on individual testing on $\beta_i$**

- $\beta_i$ is a $t$-test
- Repeated testing $\beta_i$  cause p-value inflation

## The Standard ANOVA Table for Regression

Statistical software (e.g., R, Python `statsmodels`, Stata, SAS) formats these calculations into an ANOVA table:

| Source of Variation | Sum of Squares ($SS$) | Degrees of Freedom ($df$) | Mean Square ($MS$) | $F$-Statistic | $p$-value |
| :--- | :-- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Regression (Model)** | $\text{SSR}$ | $k$ | $\text{MSR} = \frac{\text{SSR}}{k}$ | $F = \frac{\text{MSR}}{\text{MSE}}$ | $P(F_{(k, n-k-1)} \ge F)$ |
| **Residual (Error)** | $\text{SSE}$ | $n - k - 1$ | $\text{MSE} = \frac{\text{SSE}}{n - k - 1}$ | — | — |
| **Total** | $\text{SST}$ | $n - 1$ | $\text{MST} = \frac{\text{SST}}{n - 1}$ | — | — |

---

## Annotated Worked Example

:::{.columns}

:::{.column width=45%}

Research purpose: Factors affecting infant birth weight ($n = 189$).

- Outcome ($Y$): bwt (Infant birth weight in grams).

:::


:::{.column width=52%}

- Predictors ($X$): Maternal age (age), 
  - maternal weight at last menstrual period (lwt),
  -  smoking status during pregnancy (smoke), 
  -  history of hypertension (ht), 
  -  uterine irritability (ui)

:::

:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

# Load MASS (pre-installed in R)
library(MASS)
data(birthwt)

# Convert binary indicator variables into explicit factors
birthwt$smoke <- factor(birthwt$smoke, labels = c("Non-Smoker", "Smoker"))
birthwt$ht    <- factor(birthwt$ht, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
birthwt$ui    <- factor(birthwt$ui, labels = c("No", "Yes"))
```

## Regression results

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
#| output: false
model <- lm(bwt ~ age + lwt + smoke + ht + ui, data = birthwt)
summary(model)
```

## Key Metrics Calculations

1. **$R^2$ Calculation:**
$$
R^2 = \frac{17469477.719 }{ 99969655.810} = 17.4\%
$$

*Interpretation:* 17.4% of the variance in biomarker reduction is explained by maternal weight at last menstrual period, baseline metabolic index, and age.

2. **Adjusted $R^2$ Calculation:**
   $$
   R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - \left( \frac{450820.645}{99969655.810/ 188} \right) = = 1 - 0.8478 = 15.2\% 
   $$
   *Interpretation:* After penalizing for adding three model parameters, the model accounts for approximately 70.2% of the variance.

## Common issues 

**Significant $F$-statistic, but no individual significant $t$-statistics**

This classic paradox typically occurs due to **severe multicollinearity**. 

- The predictors are highly correlated with each other.
- The overall $F$-test confirms that the set of predictors collectively accounts for substantial variation.

**Low $R^2$ with a Statistically Significant $F$-test**

- **Common in noisy biological or social science data** (e.g., $R^2 = 0.08$, $p < 0.001$ with $n = 5,000$).
- This means the effect is genuine, real, and reproducible (not a sampling artifact), but individual-level variation remains high due to unmeasured factors.

# L.I.N.E Assumptions

## Overview

| Letter | Assumption | Primary Diagnostic Tool |
|:------------------:|:----------------|:----------------|:----------------|
| **L** | **Linearity** of the conditional expectation | $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid X] = 0$ | Residuals vs. Fitted Plot |
| **I** | **Independence** of observational errors | $\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0 \quad (\forall i \neq j)$ | Autocorrelation / Study Design Review |
| **N** | **Normality** of error distribution | $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ | Normal Q-Q Plot  |
| **E** | **Equal Variance** (Homoscedasticity) | $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2$ (constant) | Scale-Location Plot  |

## Pitfalls to Avoid

1. **Confusing $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ with Causality:** A high $R^2$ indicates strong linear correlation, not causal direction.
2. **Comparing $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ Across Different Transformations:** You cannot compare the $R^2$ of a model predicting $Y$ directly to a model predicting $\ln(Y)$, because $\text{SST}$ is measured on fundamentally different scales.
3. **Over-reliance on $R^2_{\text{adj}}$ Alone:** Always inspect residual diagnostics (residual vs. fitted plots, Q-Q plots) to ensure linearity, normality, and homoscedasticity assumptions hold.

## 4. In-Depth Diagnostics, Clinical Risks & Remedies

```         
                THE 4 BASE R DIAGNOSTIC PLOTS: plot(model)
   ┌───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 1. Residuals vs Fitted            │ 2. Normal Q-Q Plot                │
   │    Checks: Linearity              │    Checks: Normality              │
   │    Ideal: Flat red line at y = 0  │    Ideal: Points follow dashed 45°│
   ├───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┤
   │ 3. Scale-Location                 │ 4. Residuals vs Leverage          │
   │    Checks: Equal Variance         │    Checks: Influential Points     │
   │    Ideal: Flat horizontal line    │    Ideal: Points inside Cook's d  │
   └───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┘
```

## L — Linearity

- The relationship between $X$ and the outcome is an additive **linear** combination. 

**Example**

- The relation between X and Y is a quadratic relation instead of a linear

**Actions**

- Add non-linear polynomial terms: e.g., $\text{Age}^2$.
- Apply logarithmic or power transformations

## 

:::{.columns}

**Tool:** **Residuals vs. Fitted Plot** 

:::{.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

plot(model, which = 1)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
set.seed(2026)
birthwt_curved <- birthwt
# Inject quadratic curvature: extreme maternal weights have disproportionate effect
birthwt_curved$bwt_curved <- 1200 + 0.12 * (birthwt_curved$lwt - 130)^2 + 
                             rnorm(nrow(birthwt_curved), mean = 0, sd = 250)

mod_linear_misspec <- lm(bwt_curved ~ lwt, data = birthwt_curved)

# Plot 1: Residuals vs Fitted (Flagging Non-Linearity)
plot(mod_linear_misspec, which = 1, 
     main = "WARNING 1: Non-Linearity\n(Residuals vs Fitted)",
     col = "#2563EB", pch = 16)
# Look for: Clear 'U-shaped' red smoother line violating zero-mean expectation!
```
:::

:::{.column}

-   **Healthy Pattern:** Residuals bounce randomly across a horizontal band centered at $y = 0$, with no distinct trend. The red smooth smoother curve is nearly flat along $y = 0$.
-   **Violation Warning:** Distinct parabolic "U-shape", inverted "U", or sinusoidal wave.


:::

:::

## I — Independence of Errors

- Knowing that Patient A has an unexpectedly high outcome provides zero information about Patient B's outcome.

-   **Example**
    -   Clustering: Patients recruited from the same hospital ward or family share correlated responses.
    -   Autocorrelation: Longitudinal measurements taken repeatedly over time on the same subject.

**Actions**

- Revise study design
- **Clustered data:** Linear Mixed-Effects Models (`lme4::lmer()`) incorporating random intercepts for clusters/centers.

---

:::{.columns}

-   **Tool:** Evaluation of study design, Residuals vs. Time/Subject ID order, or **Durbin-Watson test** (`car::dwt(model)`).

:::{.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

car::dwt(model)

```

:::

:::{.column}


**Consequence**

-   **Deceptive Precision:** The effective sample size is smaller than $n$. Linear regression underestimate standard errors ($SE(\hat{\beta})$), causing artificially narrow 95% CIs.


:::

:::

## N — Normality of Residuals

- The error terms re normally distributed around the fitted line.

**Crucial Clarification:** In regression, the raw variables $Y$ and $X$ **do not** need to be normally distributed; only the **residuals** ($\varepsilon_i$) must be normally distributed.

-  **Tool:** **Normal Q-Q Plot** (Base R Plot 2: `plot(model, which = 2)`).
-  **Healthy Pattern:** Residual quantiles fall tightly along the theoretical 45-degree dashed line.

**Actions**

- Transform the outcome variable: logarithmic transformation: $$\log(Y_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i$$

## 

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

plot(model, which = 2)

```


```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
birthwt_skewed <- birthwt
# Simulate exponential right-skewed lab measurement
birthwt_skewed$nicu_stay <- rexp(nrow(birthwt_skewed), rate = 0.05)

mod_non_normal <- lm(nicu_stay ~ age + lwt + smoke, data = birthwt_skewed)

# Plot 2: Normal Q-Q Plot (Flagging Severe Non-Normality)
plot(mod_non_normal, which = 2, 
     main = "WARNING 2: Severe Right Skew\n(Normal Q-Q Plot)",
     col = "#D97706", pch = 16)
# Look for: Points strongly curving off the diagonal line at the upper right tail!
```
:::

:::{.column}

-   **Violation Warning:**
    -   **Heavy tails (S-shape):** Data has far more extreme clinical outliers than predicted by a normal curve.
    -   **Curvature at ends:** Skewed distributions (frequently seen with right-skewed lab markers such as serum creatinine, viral loads, or cytokine concentrations).

:::

:::

## E — Equal Variance 

- The variance of the residuals $\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i \mid X) = \sigma^2$ is constant across all predicted values $\hat{Y}$. (Homoscedasticity)

**Consequence**

-   Conventional $SE(\hat{\beta})$ calculations are invalid. If variance expands at higher values, standard errors are underestimated for higher exposures, leading to false claims of significance.

**Actions**

1.  **Variance-stabilizing transformations:** $\log(Y)$ or $\sqrt{Y}$.
2.  **Heteroscedasticity-Consistent (HC) Robust Standard Errors:** Using `sandwich::vcovHC(model, type = "HC3")` paired with `lmtest::coeftest()`.
3.  **Weighted Least Squares (WLS):** Weights inversely proportional to variance: $w_i = 1/\sigma_i^2$.


##

:::{.columns}

:::{.column}
-   **Tool:** **Scale-Location Plot** (Base R Plot 3: `plot(model, which = 3)`)

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

plot(model, which = 3)

```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
birthwt_hetero <- birthwt
# Error standard deviation scales directly with maternal weight (lwt)
noise_scale <- (birthwt_hetero$lwt / mean(birthwt_hetero$lwt))^2
birthwt_hetero$bwt_hetero <- 2000 + 6.5 * birthwt_hetero$lwt + 
                             rnorm(nrow(birthwt_hetero), mean = 0, sd = 180 * noise_scale)

mod_hetero <- lm(bwt_hetero ~ lwt, data = birthwt_hetero)

# Plot 3: Scale-Location Plot (Flagging Heteroscedasticity)
plot(mod_hetero, which = 3, 
     main = "WARNING 3: Unequal Variance\n(Scale-Location Plot)",
     col = "#DC2626", pch = 16)
# Look for: Red line sloping upward and point dispersion expanding into a cone/fan!
```
:::

:::{.column}


-   **Healthy Pattern:** A horizontal smooth red line with an even, constant vertical scatter of points across all fitted values.
-   **Violation Warning:** A **megaphone / funnel shape** where residual spread widens drastically as $\hat{Y}$ increases (common in biomedical dosing and growth studies).

:::


:::

## Summary Diagnostic Flowchart

```text
                      [Fit Linear Model: lm(Y ~ X1 + X2)]
                                       │
                ┌──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┐
                ▼                                             ▼
       [Evaluate Goodness-of-Fit]                    [Validate L.I.N.E.]
       • R² & Adjusted R²                            • Residuals vs Fitted (Linearity)
       • Residual Std Error (RSE)                    • Study structure (Independence)
       • Global ANOVA F-Test                         • Normal Q-Q (Normality)
                │                                    • Scale-Location (Equal Variance)
                │                                             │
                └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                                       │
                     All L.I.N.E. Assumptions Hold?
                                       │
                      ├─── YES ──► Report slopes, 95% CIs & p-values
                      │
                      └─── NO  ──► Apply Diagnostic Remedy:
                                   • Non-linear? ──► Log(X), Polynomials
                                   • Heteroscedastic? ──► Log(Y), HC3 Robust SE
                                   • Non-normal? ──► Transform Y, Bootstrap
                                   • Clustered? ──► Mixed-Effects Model (lmer)
```
